lesson.title: Racing to Infinity: Applying L'Hopital to Infinity Over Infinity
lesson.summary: Comparing how fast the numerator and denominator race off to infinity settles a whole family of growth rate questions, from logarithms to exponentials.
lesson.body:
The infinity/infinity form uses the exact same rule and the exact same conditions as 0/0, only the starting shape is different: both the numerator and the denominator grow without bound instead of both shrinking to zero. Confirm the form, differentiate top and bottom separately, recheck, and repeat if the new ratio is still indeterminate.

Consider the limit as x approaches infinity of ln(x)/x. As x grows large, ln(x) grows without bound and so does x, giving infinity/infinity. Differentiating: the derivative of ln x is 1/x, and the derivative of x is 1, giving the limit of (1/x)/1, which is the limit of 1/x as x approaches infinity. Since 1/x shrinks toward 0 as x grows, the limit equals 0. In plain language, logarithmic growth is so much slower than linear growth that ln(x) becomes negligible compared to x itself as x gets large.

A harder example needs two rounds. Consider the limit as x approaches infinity of x^2/e^x. Both x^2 and e^x grow without bound, so this is infinity/infinity. Differentiating once: the derivative of x^2 is 2x, and the derivative of e^x is e^x, giving the limit of 2x/e^x. Substituting large x still gives infinity/infinity, since 2x and e^x both still grow without bound, so differentiate again: the derivative of 2x is 2, and the derivative of e^x is e^x, giving the limit of 2/e^x. As x approaches infinity, e^x grows without bound, so 2/e^x shrinks toward 0. The limit equals 0.

That last result proves something worth remembering well beyond this one problem: exponential functions eventually outgrow every power of x, no matter how large the power, and a polynomial in the denominator would only require more rounds of differentiation, not a different outcome. This growth ordering, logarithmic growth slower than polynomial growth slower than exponential growth, shows up constantly in later mathematics and in computer science, and L'Hopital's Rule is exactly the tool that proves it rigorously rather than just asserting it by intuition.
